problem: Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}$ for the polar curve $r=2,$ given that $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\operatorname{cot}⁡(\theta ).$

activity_context.topic_title: Further Differentiation of Curves Given in Polar Form

feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{d}^{2}y}{d{x}^{2}}=\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{d\theta })}.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we need to find $\frac{dy}{dx}$ and $\frac{dx}{d\theta }.$ 

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

as parametric equations of a curve in terms of $\theta .$ 

Using the fact that $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we get

$$
x=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ),\,y=3{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Then, to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ we use the rule

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(\theta )}{{x}^{′}(\theta )}.
$$

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ),\,{y}^{′}(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}=\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ).
$$

Finally, substituting into our formula for the second derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{d\theta }(\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\theta ))}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2{sec}^{2}⁡(2\theta )}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{sec}^{3}⁡(2\theta ).\end{aligned}
$$
